newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Favourable EU ruling seen for Italy's euro tax.
newsitem.headline: Favourable EU ruling seen for Italy's euro tax.

text.p: Italy's controversial euro-tax, a one-off budgetary measure designed to secure Rome's entry into a common currency, is expected to be nodded through by the European Union on Friday, analysts said.

A negative verdict by Eurostat, the EU office responsible for overseeing government accounting practices, would virtually end Italy's hopes of becoming a founding member of economic and monetary union (EMU), expected in 1999.
"A negative decision from Eurostat would worsen the scenario," said Andrea Conti, analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Milan.
"It would make it much more difficult for Italy," he added.

With Italy's bid for a timely entry into EMU facing renewed scepticism in financial markets -- fuelled partly by Germany's well-advertised resistance to such an outcome -- the decision on the tax has become almost a watershed event.
At issue is a levy of 5.5 trillion lire ($3.2 billion) which would allow Italian taxpayers a share in the future privatisation of public companies.
In some quarters it has been criticised as a loan and therefore not in keeping with EU accounting rules. An early reading of the tax said it would be paid back to the public once Italy joined EMU.
But analysts said the measure, which is only applicable in 1997 and amounts to about 0.3 percent of GDP, has been misinterpreted because of early comments by Italian politicians.
"The bottom line is that I don't expect any big surprise," said Ilaria Fornari, economist at J.P. Morgan in Milan.
"I'm sure it was never written on paper that the tax would be reimbursed.

Even if the tax proposal is approved, EU officials caution that a decision on Italy's qualification for monetary union rests on a host of factors, most importantly the durability of its budget consolidation efforts.
When viewed in this sense, the tax may fall far short of convincing some of Italy's EU partners that it meets one of the more important principles of Maastricht.

Also at stake is a Eurostat judgment on Italian government assistance to state railways. The amount under review is considerably less -- about 3.0 trillion lire or just under 0.2 percent of output -- but here again, experts said they did not see much difficulty.
Under the plan, the government has proposed separating the principal and interest of the loans given to the state-run railway, a strategy analysts say would lessen the level of outstanding debt.
The annual deficit, however, would not be affected.
"I think both decisions will be favourable to Italy," said Filippo Cartiglia, international economist at Goldman Sachs in London.
While most economists expect the EU rulings to keep Italy on course to meet the Maastricht target, they acknowledged that further measures might be needed.
On Wednesday, Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi announced that a new mini-budget will be launched in the coming weeks, with the size of the package still to be determined.

In January, Eurostat approved a series of budgetary measures, including the treatment of interest on zero coupon bonds and postal bonds. The latter helped to knock 0.3 percent off Italy's projected deficit-to-GDP ratio, bringing it down to 3.0 percent, the Maastricht target.
At the time, Eurostat also ruled on the use of gold sales, saying the proceeds from such sales could only be used to reduce outstanding public debt, not deficits.
This was of particular relevance to Belgium and the Netherlands, two countries which have recently admitted to such sales.
Eurostat's treatment of state guarantees for public sector companies may also have an influence on Germany's 1997 fiscal outlook, but the sums involved remain unclear, experts said. ($1 = 1683 lire)
